They get huge, chewy, self-explanatory monologues in the second. Despite minor early line-fluffs from Cox and Clarkson on opening night, Jeremy Herrin’s production is full of pathos and ruined grandeur, with superb performances all round.
Herrin and his cast plot this course with caring, painstaking clarity.
Watching these fine actors bring to life a family wrecked by addiction, their love for one another corroded by hatred, is sad but also weirdly uplifting.
Brian Cox's tyrannical Tyrone is a masterclass in impotent rage

The almost three-and-a-half hours of Jeremy Herrin's production do weigh heavily, as the four members of the tormented Tyrone family, variously addicted to alcohol, drugs and self-delusion, each seek their own oblivion.
The wounds look grave, not – as they should – fatal.
This is the ultimate family reckoning, with some light, but mostly shade.
...mostly this is a very straight production. It remains a truly great play
Brian Cox puts in the work but it's a tough job

Eugene O’Neill’s 1941 autobiographical American drama, now starring Brian Cox as an actor-manager and patriarch of a dysfunctional family, is sometimes hailed as one of the greatest plays of the 20th century. But at three-and-a half hours, it’s also an ultra-marathon of misery that can be mind-bogglingly exhausting.
O’Neill’s play...in the hands of such a talented cast...it is powerful theatre.
These are fine performances in a clear-headed production of a major work that finds humour at many points, however dark it is overall.
It's a slow burner, running three hours plus interval, but not a second is wasted in Jeremy Herrin's fine production.
This is a fine production...and Herrin's direction keeps it feeling relatively fresh
...it has a remarkable capacity to speak to all times, all places and all families.
O'Neill masterwork is once again driven by its Mary
Led by Brian Cox and Patricia Clarkson, Jeremy Herrin's West End cast of soloists is definitely strong. Overall, however, his production doesn't fully sustain the tricky balancing act.
Brian Cox captures this gruff and friendless ogre very well, but the play is an unbearable torment.
At three and a half hours it's a long haul but Jeremy Herrin's clean, uncluttered production is constantly engaging.

cn.t: A solid, if conventional production elevated by strong performances, particularly Brian Cox's commanding Tyrone. Critics praise the acting's power and emotional depth, though some find the staging overly straightforward.
